title: Behavioral Activity Rating échelle (BARS)
formula:
BARS contains a single-item question consisting of seven categories:

| Behavior | Scale |
| --- | --- |
| Difficult or unable to rouse | 1 |
| Asleep but responds to verbal or physical contact | 2 |
| Drowsy, appears sedated | 3 |
| Quiet and awake (normal level of activity) | 4 |
| Signs of overt (physical or verbal) activity, calms down with instruction | 5 |
| Extremely or continuously active, not requiring restraint | 6 |
| Violent, requires restraint | 7 |

how_to_use.why:
- BARS is easy for physicians and nurses to understand and use in the acute setting, with very high inter- and intra-rater reliability.
- Unlike most other scores used to assess agitation and psychiatric symptoms, BARS has been validated in the emergency department for rapidly assessing response to a single behavioral or pharmacologic intervention.
how_to_use.when: The BARS calculator can be used in the emergency department and/or other acute care settings to rapidly assess agitation severity and response to treatment.
how_to_use.pearls:
- BARS uses psychomotor and behavioral activity as a proxy for agitation. Although this does not capture all components of agitation, it is the most clinically relevant aspect of agitation in the acute setting.
- The score is based on clinical observation and does not require participation from the patient.
- Although BARS can assess the behavioral response to acute interventions, it does not distinguish between medical and psychiatric etiologies of agitation.
- Suggested actions in response to BARS scores are based on expert[consensus guidelines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3298208/)from the American Association of Emergency Psychiatry.

next_steps.advice:
- BARS can be reassessed at multiple time points after an intervention for agitation.
- Given its ease of use and strong inter-rater reliability, any clinical team member at the bedside with the patient can report a BARS score.
next_steps.critical_actions:
- Attempt verbal de-escalation with patients with BARS 5-6 before resorting to chemical or physical restraints.
- Broaden the differential diagnosis to include possible medical causes of sedation or agitation in patients with BARS 1-3 or 7.
- Patients with BARS 1 require close monitoring regardless of the etiology of their behavioral state.
next_steps.management:
BARS is a seven-point scale with scores ranging from 1 to 7.Scores are assigned based on a single clinical observation.

- BARS 1-3: Additional medical workup may be needed.
- BARS 4: Likely normal behavioral activity, intervention not needed.
- BARS 5-6: Indicate the need for verbal de-escalation or other behavioral interventions.
- BARS 7: Patient likely to require pharmacologic intervention and/or physical restraints. May require additional medical workup.

evidence:
The[original](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11777497/)study was a secondary analysis of data from three U.S.-based randomized controlled trials with a total of 502 patients, evaluating intramuscular ziprasidone for agitation in patients with psychosis. In this analysis, BARS showed strong correlation with two established agitation scales, CGI-S and PANSS. Notably, BARS outperformed these measures in detecting changes in agitation over a four-hour period following treatment. It also had near-perfect inter- and intra-rater reliability.

It has also been[validated](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35129902/)in Portuguese and found to correlate with the Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS), a similar seven-point clinical observation score used primarily in the ICU setting.

BARS has been incorporated into[protocols](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3298208/)suggested by the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry, with scores of 5-7 requiring verbal de-escalation or pharmacologic intervention.
